title: Couch Crew
user: Friends in one room who want a 20-minute cooperative party game where every phone has a meaningful, different role.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Gaming Couch commenter specifically wanted a modern take on Pokémon Stadium-style minigames; the maker says an open game-development ecosystem is still planned.
Gaming Couch is a live no-account browser party platform for up to eight phone controllers, validating setup appetite while concentrating on competitive mini-games.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 discussions around browser couch play; the repeated complaint is that Jackbox-style prompts are not satisfying action games.
current_workaround: Buy Jackbox packs, pass controllers around, or settle for competitive microgames with a TV browser.
incumbents_and_gap: Gaming Couch, AirConsole, and Jackbox solve connection/setup, but mostly offer collections of competitive rounds. A short cooperative role campaign is absent.
smallest_useful_product: A one-screen, 3–6 player 18-minute heist: driver, lookout, hacker, loader, and dispatcher use two-button phone controls through three escalating missions. Non-goals: a game platform, voice chat, accounts, or a user-generated-content SDK.
success_measure: At least 35% of rooms start a second mission within 24 hours and median room completion exceeds 14 minutes.
monetization: free — frictionless room links are the product; a paid seasonal mission pack is only worth considering after repeat-play evidence.
constraints: Use short room codes and anonymous ephemeral sessions; no copyrighted character or minigame imitation; support touch and keyboard fallback.
why_distinct: The unit is an asymmetric cooperative run, not another trivia pack or a generic party-game portal.

title: Bridge Crew
user: Teachers and youth-group hosts who need a room-code cooperative game playable from a shared display while each participant uses a school browser—not a phone app—as their controller.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A commenter asks for party games where browsers, rather than phones, are controllers for schools, and calls out Star Trek bridge simulations as a desired form.
Sim Drive is a current multiplayer browser racing simulator built around phone controllers, illustrating the existing phone-first default.

recurrence: The school constraint is explicit and materially different from living-room phone play: managed devices and laptops are already open.
current_workaround: Use a slide deck and verbal roles, install a game, or try phone-controller party sites that are unsuitable for managed classroom devices.
incumbents_and_gap: Sim Drive and Gaming Couch expect phones; Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes requires a purchased desktop game and printed material. Browser-controlled collaborative stations are thin.
smallest_useful_product: A 4–8 player, 12-minute spaceship-repair run: participants join with a code in any browser, receive complementary panels, and coordinate repairs on the projected bridge. Non-goals: curriculum management, student accounts, or AI narration.
success_measure: In five pilot rooms, 80% of participants join in under 90 seconds without host-side troubleshooting and 3+ rooms voluntarily replay.
monetization: free — schools should be able to test it without procurement; optional one-time facilitator scenario pack later.
constraints: No chat, recording, or personal data; keyboard-only accessibility; room state must expire automatically; content must be classroom-safe.
why_distinct: It treats each browser tab as an asymmetrical game station, rather than shrinking a phone controller onto a laptop.

title: Pocket Draft Duel
user: Two to four friends who want a 15-minute tactical card-game session by room code, with a new fair draft each run and no collection, login, or deck building beforehand.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Discussion of The Deck says a compelling digital game-night use case is letting people create and share their own game rules, while another commenter values one-host/scan-to-join setup.
The Deck is an open-source mobile turn-by-turn card-game engine, demonstrating infrastructure exists but not a focused browser game built around a fresh short-session draft.

recurrence: Game-night participants repeatedly value no-search, one-host joining and flexible rules, yet general engines leave the actual approachable game to somebody else.
current_workaround: Bring a physical deck, install a card app, or teach a longer collectible-card game.
incumbents_and_gap: The Deck, Board Game Arena, and Codenames-style sites support particular games or engines; they do not offer a browser-native micro-draft whose preparation is the game.
smallest_useful_product: Room-code 2–4 player simultaneous draft of 18 public-domain-icon cards, then three three-minute battles with one chosen tactic per round. Non-goals: collectible cards, ranked ladder, chat, or custom-card publishing.
success_measure: 60% of completed rooms launch a rematch and median time from URL open to first pick is below two minutes.
monetization: one-time — a modest host unlock for additional balanced draft sets fits a contained game better than a recurring charge.
constraints: Use original/public-domain art only; server-authoritative simultaneous picks; do not create a gambling-like economy or paid random packs.
why_distinct: It turns the shared draft into a complete, repeatable run instead of recreating a collectible card game or generic engine.

title: Route of the Day
user: Daily-puzzle regulars who want one fresh five-minute spatial route puzzle plus an optional archive and practice mode, without another word or chess clone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN explicitly requests free, web-based daily games with a new puzzle every day and lists mostly word games, signaling demand for more variety in that habit.
Gerrymandle is a live daily map-drawing puzzle; its HN discussion includes requests for a more approachable interactive tutorial.

recurrence: An explicit 2026 request for additions to a daily-web-game routine, plus engagement with a new non-word daily puzzle, indicates a repeat habit rather than a one-off novelty.
current_workaround: Cycle through Wordle descendants, chess puzzles, and daily sites that often offer only one domain or block practice behind completion.
incumbents_and_gap: NYT Games, Puzzmo, and Gerrymandle demonstrate the ritual, but the field is crowded with language and number puzzles and sparse in accessible spatial routing.
smallest_useful_product: A deterministic daily grid where players lay 6–10 route tiles to connect landmarks under one changing constraint; after completion, unlimited non-scored archived seeds unlock. Non-goals: social feed, streak punishments, news/political simulation, or account requirement.
success_measure: 25% seven-day return among anonymous daily solvers and at least 20% of first-day finishers try an archive puzzle.
monetization: free — daily puzzle discovery needs sharing and no-login access; sponsorship is only viable after a sustained audience.
constraints: Publish seed and solution deterministically; provide color-independent symbols and reduced-motion mode; avoid real electoral data or political claims.
why_distinct: A route-building spatial puzzle fills a daily-web-game gap without copying Wordle’s answer-checking loop.

title: Tide & Tile
user: Casual daily players who want a calm, satisfying two-to-five-minute tactile puzzle with an honest share result and a clear difficulty ramp.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gerrymandle players ask for introductory levels of increasing difficulty and report that the initial puzzle takes time to understand.
Rotaboxes is a live relaxing daily photo-rotation puzzle that displays clicks and an ideal count, validating short tactile daily play rather than only word guessing.

recurrence: Daily-puzzle commenters independently praise the idea but request onboarding; the existing rotation game demonstrates a compact low-stakes session format.
current_workaround: Play a daily word game, hunt for puzzle explanations, or abandon a novel mechanic when the first board is too opaque.
incumbents_and_gap: Rotaboxes has a relaxing rotation mechanic; common daily games have streaks and steep implicit rules. There is room for a daily physical-feeling mechanic designed around learnability.
smallest_useful_product: A daily 4×4 tide board: tap tiles to rotate their water channels, make one continuous harbor route, and earn optional 'fewest turns' medals. First three visits use progressive micro-tutorials; archive boards are always available. Non-goals: photo licensing, leaderboards, lives, or accounts.
success_measure: 90% of first-time players solve the tutorial board without opening help; 30% return on day two.
monetization: free — the lightweight game benefits from casual sharing; paid cosmetics would undermine the calming premise.
constraints: Original SVG art and generated boards only; colorblind-safe water states; offline cache must not invalidate the daily seed.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately teachable tactile ritual, not a photo scramble or word-puzzle clone.

title: Mirror Orchard
user: Puzzle players who like novel visual mechanics but want past puzzles and a low-pressure way to learn them instead of being locked into a single daily attempt.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the Hidden Mirrors discussion, a player explicitly says they always wish daily puzzle games had an archive of past puzzles; another says they would open all puzzles rather than wait for daily cadence.
Hidden Mirrors is a live visual-symmetry game with a daily puzzle, showing appetite for nonverbal mechanics but not resolving the archive request.

recurrence: Two commenters in one substantive play thread independently ask for more accessible availability, an acute issue for novel mechanics where the daily board is also the tutorial.
current_workaround: Wait until tomorrow, watch a solution, or bounce to familiar Wordle-like games.
incumbents_and_gap: Hidden Mirrors and daily puzzle portals establish the format, but daily gating forces a first impression to carry all learning and excludes players who miss a day.
smallest_useful_product: A seed-based visual symmetry game about growing a mirrored orchard: one daily featured puzzle plus an always-open, ordered archive of 40 teaching boards and replayable personal seeds. Non-goals: endless procedural content, leaderboard pressure, or a clone of Hidden Mirrors' transformation rules.
success_measure: At least half of new players finish three archived teaching boards before attempting the daily puzzle, with 20% returning within a week.
monetization: free — archive access is central to usefulness, not a subscription gate.
constraints: Invent an independently designed symmetry rule and visual language; make every state distinguishable without color; preserve seed reproducibility.
why_distinct: The product resolves the daily-puzzle learning trap through a curated playable archive rather than simply publishing another daily puzzle.

title: Last Lap Breakout
user: People on a short break who want a run-based action game they can finish in under ten minutes, with meaningful build choices but no endless grind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Players of a Breakout roguelite report playing several rounds and engage with its perk system; feedback focuses on clarity of the run’s reward loop.
Breakout 71 is a live browser Breakout game, evidence that a low-input arcade core can carry a roguelite-style session on the web.

recurrence: The play thread contains actual repeat-round behavior and detailed perk feedback, not hypothetical interest, while the one-input core keeps browser entry light.
current_workaround: Open a roguelite with a 30–60 minute commitment, play an unstructured arcade high-score game, or use a mobile app.
incumbents_and_gap: Vampire Survivors-style games and Breakout 71 supply action or builds, but generally leave session length open-ended. A deliberately finite browser run is rarer.
smallest_useful_product: Eight fixed 60-second laps of paddle-and-orb play. After each lap choose one of three readable modifiers; lap eight is a designed boss and ends the run with a shareable build string. Non-goals: meta-progression, ads between laps, battle pass, or infinite survival.
success_measure: Median first-session completion reaches lap six and 30% of finishers start another run with a different modifier path.
monetization: free — the honest finite run is the differentiator; small one-time alternate challenge sets can be tested later.
constraints: Original physics, names, and art; touch and keyboard parity; no flashing effects without reduced-motion setting; keep deterministic replay hashes.
why_distinct: It commits to a visible eight-minute ending, rather than using roguelite upgrades to prolong a familiar arcade game indefinitely.

title: Finite Forge
user: Incremental-game fans who enjoy planning a reset but want a satisfying browser game with a real 30–45 minute ending rather than an endless retention loop.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Bitburner player describes the satisfaction of starting simple, discovering a new method, then cleanly resetting to do a better next run; another notes it works poorly on mobile.
Bitburner is a live programming-based incremental game, confirming web incremental play and reset-driven mastery, but it is a large ongoing game rather than a contained mobile-friendly session.

recurrence: The reset loop is explicitly praised by players, while a mobile complaint identifies a web-session usability gap.
current_workaround: Leave an endless idle game open for days, follow opaque optimization guides, or play large programming incrementals on desktop.
incumbents_and_gap: Bitburner, Evolve, and Cookie Clicker offer deep infinite economies. They rarely promise an ending that respects one evening and one thumb.
smallest_useful_product: A portrait browser forge in which 24 production ticks build one beacon before a sunset deadline. Each reset unlocks exactly one new tool and the final beacon ends the campaign after 4–6 runs. Non-goals: real-time offline accumulation, premium currency, social pressure, scripting, or infinite prestige layers.
success_measure: At least 40% of new players reach a first reset and 25% complete the final beacon within seven days without a guide.
monetization: one-time — a finite handcrafted campaign can be sold transparently as an optional full unlock after a free first run.
constraints: Avoid dark-pattern timers and fake scarcity; make all numbers readable on a phone; no copyrighted industrial-game assets; store progress locally by default.
why_distinct: It borrows the pleasurable reset insight while deliberately ending, instead of optimizing for indefinite idle retention.

title: Tap Trail
user: Rhythm-game fans on locked-down computers or phones who want two-minute precise input challenges in a browser without downloads, accounts, copyrighted music, or video permissions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: DanceJump is presented as turning YouTube videos into a browser rhythm game, making the desire for web rhythm play explicit but tying it to third-party video and extension distribution.
The live DanceJump distribution is a Chrome Web Store extension, demonstrating the current install and YouTube dependency that a plain web game can avoid.

recurrence: A current browser rhythm project uses an extension and external music/video catalog—useful validation, but also clear friction and licensing exposure.
current_workaround: Install an extension, use a desktop rhythm client, or play video-synced web experiences with variable timing and rights constraints.
incumbents_and_gap: osu!, Bemuse, and DanceJump offer rhythm play; DanceJump’s YouTube/extension path and user-song ecosystems carry compatibility and rights complexity. A compact original-audio browser option is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A no-login tap/keyboard rhythm game with 30 original 90-second percussion tracks, deterministic daily charts, latency calibration, and three visible difficulty lanes. Non-goals: YouTube import, user music uploads, licensed songs, ranked matchmaking, or a native app.
success_measure: 80% of first-time players complete calibration and 25% replay the same track to improve a score in their first visit.
monetization: one-time — a small original track pack can be purchased without ads or music-rights ambiguity.
constraints: Commission or create all audio with clear licenses; offer audio-offset calibration and reduced-motion mode; do not collect microphone data.
why_distinct: It is a legally clean, latency-conscious micro-rhythm game—not an upload wrapper around somebody else’s videos or songs.

title: One Screen Sprint
user: Two people at one keyboard who want an immediate competitive five-minute game with readable controls and a fresh procedural course each match.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN explicitly seeks browser games that are engaging, sensory, reaction-based, and exciting rather than turn-based or story-heavy; replies note weak web implementations and performance problems.
A live browser shooter’s HN play discussion reports that it loads on an iPhone and held a player’s attention for 20 minutes, validating fast browser action without an install.

recurrence: An explicit game-finder request defines a still-unmet browser use case, while real player feedback shows immediate browser action can hold attention when it loads cleanly.
current_workaround: Play Slither-like games alone, open a desktop multiplayer title, or use a browser shooter that requires a public server and network conditions.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser shooters serve remote play and arcade portals serve solo scores; simple same-keyboard action with guaranteed short matches is comparatively neglected.
smallest_useful_product: A two-player local side-view dash-and-grapple race. One player uses WASD, the other arrows; a procedurally assembled 75-second course changes each best-of-five match. Non-goals: guns, online matchmaking, chat, account profiles, or user-created levels.
success_measure: 70% of sessions finish a full best-of-five and 40% generate a second course without leaving the page.
monetization: free — it is a shareable zero-friction game; no ads should interrupt a 75-second round.
constraints: Test focus handling and key rollover; touch is not a v1 promise; use original art/sound; include seizure-safe effects settings.
why_distinct: It serves physical co-presence with one keyboard, not the much more common online shooter queue.

title: Practice After Daily
user: Special-interest daily-puzzle players who want the shared daily challenge but also a no-pressure practice run that teaches the domain after they finish.

evidence.quote_or_summary: GeneGuessr’s creator explains that practice mode unlocks after the daily puzzle; a commenter asks how to enable it and whether it offers more hints and guesses for newcomers.
GeneGuessr is a live daily protein-guessing web game, validating a niche-knowledge daily format and revealing the discoverability cost of hidden practice.

recurrence: The maker built practice because a daily-only puzzle excludes learning; a separate player immediately needed clearer access and gentler rules.
current_workaround: Google explanations, wait for another daily, or give up after an opaque specialized puzzle.
incumbents_and_gap: GeneGuessr and subject-specific daily puzzles prove that a domain can sustain a ritual, but practice is often secondary or locked behind the main solve.
smallest_useful_product: A daily 'Signal Garden' classification puzzle: infer a fictional ecosystem from compact traits, receive semantic feedback, then choose an openly visible practice seed with optional hints and a short explanation. Non-goals: real biology claims, scraped datasets, classroom dashboards, or LLM answers.
success_measure: At least 30% of daily starters use practice, and practice users have a 20-point higher next-day completion rate than non-practice users.
monetization: free — educational clarity and sharing matter more than gating hints; a donation link is sufficient for v1.
constraints: Use fictional/generated taxonomy to avoid misinformation; show accessible explanations; local anonymous progress only; no health or scientific advice.
why_distinct: The practice loop is visible from the start and is part of the game’s learning design, not a buried consolation mode.

title: Room Code Mystery
user: Remote friend groups who want a warm, low-stakes 20-minute social deduction game with a room code, no pack purchase, and no AI-generated judgments.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A commenter says they are not a fan of Jackbox’s pack distribution model while discussing a casual platform that supports in-person or video-chat multiplayer.
Gametje is a live casual multiplayer platform for central-screen or video-chat play, showing demand for simple remote-friendly browser rooms but not a focused single game.

recurrence: A direct distribution-model objection appears alongside a working casual platform: people want the social session, not repeated pack purchasing or portal browsing.
current_workaround: Buy a Jackbox pack, schedule a Discord game, or hunt through a general game portal for a room-compatible title.
incumbents_and_gap: Jackbox, Gametje, and Death by AI offer broad party catalogues or AI novelty. A self-contained, rules-light room-code mystery with human adjudication is still a useful wedge.
smallest_useful_product: A 4–8 player browser mystery told in three timed evidence rounds. Each player receives different visual clues; the group submits one accusation before a compact reveal. One host shares a code, remote players use personal views. Non-goals: public matchmaking, voice/video, LLM judging, permanent accounts, or a game portal.
success_measure: 50% of rooms complete all three rounds and 25% start a second case in the same gathering.
monetization: one-time — sell additional handcrafted cases to the host, with the starter case fully playable free.
constraints: Write original cases and art; no user-generated accusations retained; design clues to avoid stereotyping; ephemeral anonymous room state.
why_distinct: It sells a complete human-authored social-deduction session, not a bundle storefront, collection site, or LLM comedy wrapper.
